title: Nagelsmann Is Out. Klopp Is In. Germany's World Cup Reckoning Just Produced Football's Biggest Coaching Move.
excerpt: A three-hour meeting in Frankfurt sealed the end. The DFB is already in talks with Jürgen Klopp, who has signalled willingness to return to the dugout for his country.
body:
Julian Nagelsmann walked into the German Football Association's Frankfurt headquarters on Thursday morning still believing he had a future. By the time he walked out, he did not.

The 38-year-old stepped down as Germany head coach after a three-hour meeting with DFB chiefs, including national team director Rudi Völler, made his position untenable. Nagelsmann was not technically sacked — he resigned — but the distinction is cosmetic. The DFB wanted him gone, and he complied.

The catalyst was clear enough: Germany's penalty shootout defeat to Paraguay in the Round of 32 on Monday in Foxborough. It was their first ever World Cup shootout loss, against a team ranked 30 places below them, on a night when every ball that bounced seemed to bounce the wrong way.

Three consecutive disappointing World Cups — group-stage exits in 2018 and 2022, a Round of 32 elimination in 2026 — made the situation unsalvageable, even for a coach who had initially transformed the national team's mood after a dismal Euro 2024 cycle.

## 'My Top Priority Has Always Been the Team's Success'

Nagelsmann, who had defiantly told reporters after the Paraguay match that he was "not someone who runs away," struck a different tone in his resignation statement.

"I've been doing a lot of thinking over the past few days," he said. "My top priority has always been the team's success. After such a bitter disappointment, they deserve the chance for a fresh start. A special thank you goes to the fans. You carried us, you trusted us, you gave us energy, even during difficult times. It truly pains me that we disappointed you."

The DFB praised his "high level of commitment and extraordinary ambition" but wasted no time in revealing the name everyone already expected.


![World Cup — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Kitzbuehel_slalom_ganslernhang_2010.jpg)



> **""I've been doing a lot of thinking over the past few days," he said."**



## Enter Klopp

The DFB confirmed on Friday that its board has opened formal conversations with Jürgen Klopp, and that the 59-year-old has signalled "general willingness" to consider the position.

Klopp has been in the United States throughout the World Cup, working as a pundit for German television. He has been asked about the Germany job repeatedly and has deflected every time, saying it was "not the right moment" — a formulation that itself hinted at interest.

The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund manager joined Red Bull as head of global soccer in early 2025, after telling the world he was done coaching. But the Germany job is different. It is understood that Klopp and Red Bull CEO Oliver Mintzlaff have a gentlemen's agreement: if the DFB called, Klopp would be free to go.

It also emerged that Pep Lijnders, Klopp's former assistant at Liverpool, would be keen to join his backroom staff. The 43-year-old Dutchman is available after leaving Manchester City following Pep Guardiola's departure.

## What Germany Gets

Klopp would inherit a squad that is not short on talent — Jamal Musiala, Florian Wirtz, Kai Havertz — but is clearly short on tournament mentality. Germany's record at major tournaments since lifting the 2014 World Cup is a catalogue of dysfunction: early exits, internal disputes, and tactical inconsistency.

Klopp built his career on exactly the opposite: relentless energy, emotional connection, and teams that believed they could run through walls. At Dortmund, he turned a mid-table club into Champions League finalists. At Liverpool, he ended a 30-year Premier League drought and built a dynasty.


![World Cups — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Kitzbuehel_slalom_ganslernhang_2010.jpg)


The question is whether that intensity — the thing that burned him out at Anfield and made him walk away from club football — can be sustained on the international stage, where the rhythms are different and the windows are narrow.

His task is clear: rebuild Germany for Euro 2028, hosted by the UK and Ireland, and the 2030 World Cup in Spain, Portugal, and Morocco.

## The Wider Shakeup

Nagelsmann is not the only coaching casualty of this World Cup. Ronald Koeman resigned as Netherlands manager this week after their own Round of 32 elimination. The tournament is barely three weeks old, and the coaching carousel is already spinning.

For the millions of football fans in the Indian diaspora across the US and UK — many of whom grew up watching Klopp's Liverpool teams dominate the Premier League and Champions League — this is not a peripheral storyline. The Bundesliga and Premier League are the two most-watched European leagues among NRIs, and Klopp is one of the most recognisable managers on the planet.

If confirmed, it would be football's most significant international coaching appointment since Pep Guardiola was linked with the Brazil job. Except Klopp appears to actually want this one.

## What Happens Next

The DFB has not set a formal deadline, but the expectation is that Klopp's appointment could be confirmed within days. Germany's next competitive fixtures are the 2028 European Championship qualifiers, which begin in March 2027.

That gives Klopp nine months to assess, rebuild, and do what he does best: make players believe they are better than they think they are.
